reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: A bunionette is a painful prominence of the lateral aspect of the fifth metatarsal head, the mirror image on the lateral border of the foot of a hallux valgus bunion
It arises from lateral bowing or deviation of the fifth metatarsal with medial deviation of the little toe, widening the forefoot laterally
The prominent metatarsal head rubs against footwear to produce a painful callosity or an inflamed adventitial bursa over the lateral eminence
It is commoner in those who wear narrow or constricting shoes and may coexist with hallux valgus as part of a splayed forefoot
Weight-bearing radiographs allow measurement of the fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal angle and lateral deviation and help classify the deformity to guide treatment
Radiographic types include a prominent fifth metatarsal head, lateral bowing of the metatarsal shaft, and an increased fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal angle
Distinguish it from a plantar-lateral keratosis, a fifth metatarsal stress lesion, and a soft-tissue mass or ganglion
Initial management is conservative with wide, soft footwear, padding of the lateral eminence, and orthoses, with lateral eminence resection or a metatarsal osteotomy reserved for persistent pain
reference.pathophysiology: A bunionette is a lateral forefoot deformity analogous to hallux valgus but affecting the fifth ray, in which the fifth metatarsal head becomes prominent laterally and the little toe deviates medially. The prominence may result from an intrinsically wide or laterally bowed fifth metatarsal, from an increased angle between the fourth and fifth metatarsals that splays the forefoot, or simply from an enlarged lateral condyle of the metatarsal head. Constricting footwear that compresses the forefoot contributes by pressing on and irritating the lateral eminence. Chronic pressure between the bony prominence and the shoe produces a reactive callosity and an inflamed adventitial bursa, which are the usual sources of pain. When the prominence is plantar as well as lateral, a plantar keratosis can develop. The deformity frequently accompanies hallux valgus and a generally splayed, broad forefoot.
additionalDifferentials: Plantar or plantar-lateral keratosis under the fifth metatarsal head
Fifth metatarsal stress fracture or other bony lesion
Ganglion or soft-tissue mass over the lateral eminence
Fifth metatarsophalangeal joint arthritis or synovitis
Infected bursa or septic arthritis of the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint
Lateral corn or intractable plantar keratosis from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and oblique foot radiographs to measure the fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal angle and lateral deviation
Classification of the deformity type on radiographs to guide surgical planning
Standing clinical examination of the lateral eminence, callosity, and associated forefoot deformity
Assessment for coexisting hallux valgus and forefoot splaying
Serum urate and inflammatory markers if crystal or inflammatory arthropathy is suspected
Vascular and neurological assessment before any planned surgery
Cross-sectional imaging only in atypical cases to characterise a soft-tissue mass or occult lesion
redFlags: A hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint suggesting septic arthritis, an infected bursa, or acute gout
Ulceration or skin breakdown over the lateral eminence, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease
Focal bony tenderness suggesting a fifth metatarsal stress fracture
A rapidly enlarging soft-tissue mass raising concern for tumour
reference.prognosis: Most bunionettes are controlled with footwear modification and padding, and symptoms often settle once pressure on the lateral eminence is relieved. When surgery is needed, lateral eminence resection or a metatarsal osteotomy chosen according to the deformity type gives good pain relief in the majority, although recurrence, transfer symptoms, or under-correction can occur, particularly if constricting footwear is resumed or the underlying angular deformity is not corrected.
pitfalls: Resecting the lateral eminence alone when an increased intermetatarsal angle requires an osteotomy, leading to recurrence
Failing to classify the deformity radiographically before planning surgery
Attributing a hot, painful joint to the bunionette and missing gout or infection
Overlooking a coexisting fifth metatarsal stress fracture as a cause of lateral pain
Neglecting footwear advice so that pressure and symptoms recur after treatment
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Modify footwear to a wide, accommodative toe-box and avoid narrow constricting shoes to relieve pressure on the lateral fifth metatarsal eminence
Offload the prominence with padding, silicone spacers or orthoses and provide callus and plantar keratosis care
Relieve pain with analgesia or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and treat the inflamed adventitial bursa
Reserve surgery for symptoms refractory to conservative care, selecting lateral eminence resection or a metatarsal osteotomy according to the radiographic deformity type
Complete vascular and neurological assessment before any planned surgery and address coexisting hallux valgus or forefoot splaying
Refer to podiatry or orthopaedic foot and ankle services for classification and operative planning
